content.heading: Custom Software for Complex Engineering Design

slides.title: Introduction
slides.subtitle: Who I am and the kind of work I do.
slides.takeaway: I turn engineering work that's repetitive and rule-based into reliable software.

notes.intent: Establish credibility and frame this as an expanding mandate, not a one-off side project.
notes.summary:
• Engineer I in Fire Suppression Technology; CS & Engineering from Lehigh; about three years in.
• Left column is what I've shipped; right column is where I'm taking it.
• Where it's going: AI for project knowledge, cloud infrastructure with IT, department-wide AI, other teams.

• Keep it to 60 to 90 seconds.
notes.bridge: So why does this kind of work even need to exist? Here's the root problem.

slides.title: The Root Problem
slides.subtitle: The real reasons capable teams keep solving new problems with the tools already on the desk.
slides.takeaway: We're not short on engineering talent — we're short on tools built for the way we actually work.

notes.intent: Win buy-in by naming the real reasons capable teams stay stuck on the tools already on the desk.
notes.summary:
• Walk the four root causes; don't just say things are hard.
• Excel overextended, tribal knowledge undocumented, the right tool is rare and costly, and plain habit.
• The 'expensive' tile sets up my reveal: it takes product depth and software skill in one person, the gap I fill.
• Keep it universal, no product names yet. Don't resolve it; let it sit.
notes.bridge: Let me show you what this actually looked like for one of our systems.

tiles.title: Excel, Overextended
tiles.description: We lean on spreadsheets to do the work of real applications, far beyond what they were ever built for.

tiles.title: Tribal Knowledge
tiles.description: The logic that matters lives in senior engineers' heads, not in anything documented or shared.

tiles.title: The Right Tool Is Expensive
tiles.description: Purpose-built software needs someone who knows the product deeply and can build software: a rare, costly combination, so it rarely gets built.

tiles.title: "We've Always Done It This Way"
tiles.description: Proven processes are comfortable, and few realize a better tool is even possible, so change is hard to justify.

slides.title: A Real Example
slides.subtitle: What designing one system used to take — and where the logic lived.
slides.takeaway: The logic was real engineering judgment — just scattered across documents that never talked to each other.

notes.intent: Make the fragmentation felt: one design used to mean four disconnected sources and no single source of truth.
notes.summary:
• Frame the product in one line: a hybrid suppression system, powerful but painful to configure.
• Open the four real artifacts live as you talk: Configurator (media, partcodes), Estimator (hand calcs), Price List, Design Manual (agency rules).
• Land it: 4+ sources that never talked to each other, so quality depended on who did the work.
• Backup: the XLSX and XLSM download, so have them already open in Excel; the PDFs open in a tab.
notes.bridge: That's what it felt like. Here's what we actually changed underneath.

content.setup: Take one of our most capable products — a hybrid suppression system. Powerful in the field, painful to configure. To assemble a single design, the rules you needed were spread across separate, disconnected documents:

sources.title: Vortex Configurator
sources.sub: Media constraints, valid configurations, and partcodes.

sources.title: Vortex Project Estimator v2.4
sources.sub: The design calculations, run by hand.

sources.title: Vortex Price List (PL2021 Rev. A)
sources.sub: Pricing, looked up and transcribed separately.

sources.title: Vortex Design Manual (VDM-VORTEX-01)
sources.sub: Agency rules, standards, and reference data, recalled from memory.

punchline.label: no single source of truth — so the result was only as good as the engineer who did it.

slides.title: Vortex Project Builder
slides.subtitle: From scattered logic to one validated tool — live.
slides.takeaway: Same inputs, same output — every engineer, every time.

notes.intent: Show the turn, restructure then encode, and prove it with a live build.
notes.summary:
• Read each Signal as how I spotted the candidate; the Target across from it is the response.
• Say the maturity line: I didn't just digitize the sheets, I restructured the method into one model, then encoded it once.
• Launch live: load a preset, define two zones, trigger a warning on purpose, export the BOM (about 7 minutes).
• Close: that BOM is audit-ready and identical for any engineer on the same inputs.
• Keep screenshots ready as backup if the demo stalls.
notes.bridge: Now, not everything needs a platform this big.

signal.v: Project complexity scaled the design-calculation complexity — all done by hand.

target.v: Handle the calculations, with transparent results so the logic can be validated — closing the calculation gap.

signal.v: Feasibility was bottlenecked by Applications Engineering and training support.

target.v: Abstracts requirements into simple inputs and enforces standards at runtime — anyone produces a compliant project.

signal.v: One estimate meant juggling async files (price list, manual, NFPA codes), job knowledge, hand calcs, and coordination across Sales, Apps Eng & Customer Care.

target.v: Price list & partcodes build the BOM alongside the config, then hand off directly to Customer Care — one flow replaces the juggle.

slides.title: VicFlex Bracket Filter
slides.subtitle: Same thinking, smaller scale — also live.
slides.takeaway: Automating the decision you make 40 times beats optimizing the one you make once.

notes.intent: Prove the same Signal-to-Target thinking scales down to a high-frequency lookup.
notes.summary:
• The pattern is familiar now, so move faster through the five pairs.
• Launch live: pick known components, watch it return compatible configurations instantly against the D-value threshold (about 6 minutes).
• Reinforce the wins: self-service for sales, no engineering gatekeeping, no training needed.
notes.bridge: Both of those followed the exact same process. Here's that process.

signal.v: The modular VicFlex line introduces thousands of possible configuration options.

target.v: A database of the most common configurations captures the space that actually matters.

signal.v: Each option carries its own compatibility requirements.

target.v: One feasibility gauge — the D-VALUE distance threshold — replaces scattered, per-option rules.

signal.v: Compatibility logic stayed locked with project and application engineers.

target.v: Navigate the database from known or desired parts — the knowledge is now queryable by anyone.

signal.v: To recommend a config, Sales had to reach out to engineering to confirm compatibility.

target.v: Sales answers compatibility themselves, instantly — no round-trip.

signal.v: Engineers spent hours each week rebuilding custom configurations to reproduce feasibility.

target.v: A familiar shopping-style interface means no training and no engineering labor to build a valid configuration.

slides.title: How I Build Internal Platforms
slides.subtitle: A cross-functional lifecycle from concept to deployment.
slides.takeaway: Alignment, validation, and iteration are what make tools scalable.

notes.intent: Answer 'how do you actually do this?' through the four principles, not a six-phase lecture.
notes.summary:
• Frame it: every tool you just saw followed this same lifecycle.
• Don't read all six phases. Use the four principles, each pairs two phases:
   - Deeply Immerse covers Discovery and Immersion
   - Prototype Fast covers Architecture and Prototype
   - All Feedback Is Valuable covers Validation Sprints
   - Leverage AI runs underneath all of it
• Name the AI tools out loud: grill-me to plan, Claude Code to build.
notes.bridge: So does this actually move the needle? Here's the measurable side.

principles.title: Deeply Immerse
principles.description: Learn the whole problem: who it affects, who actually uses it, the assumptions hiding in the old workflow, and the data that reveals the pattern.

principles.title: Prototype Fast
principles.description: Get to a working build fast, even a wrong one. It's hard to critique a concept while the workflow itself is changing; a real prototype gives people something concrete to react to.

principles.title: All Feedback Is Valuable
principles.description: Cross-functional testing surfaces every use case. A complaint or a suggestion is signal: the tool improves, and it never adds a learning curve.

principles.title: Leverage AI
principles.description: Use AI to capture the idea, surface blind spots, and turn a clear plan into a working prototype, fast.

slides.title: Where the Effort Goes
slides.subtitle: How effort behaves, the old way versus now.
slides.takeaway: The more complex the work, the wider the gap, and the more the tool saves.

notes.intent: Show the shape of the savings, backed by one real, measured proof.
notes.summary:
• Be upfront: the left chart is an illustrative model, the right is measured.
• Vortex (left): old cost accelerates (calc per enclosure, then a hand-built BOM, then slower pricing), the builder stays flat, so the gap widens with complexity.
• VicFlex (right): 156 engineering hours recovered a year (2 requests per week, 1.5 hours each, 52 weeks).
• Make it human: each request was a focused interruption into SolidWorks; now Sales self-serves in under five minutes.
notes.bridge: And this is where I want your help.

curve.title: Vortex: Effort vs. Complexity
curve.caption: Each enclosure used to add its own calc, BOM, and pricing work, so cost accelerated. The builder absorbs complexity in one codified step, so effort stays flat and the gap widens.

recovery.title: VicFlex: Engineering Hours Recovered
recovery.caption: Each request used to pull an engineer into SolidWorks to verify geometry and D-value compatibility; the tool returns it in under five minutes. The recovered time compounds across the year.

slides.title: Is This Your Workflow?
slides.subtitle: Maybe there's a better way.
slides.takeaway: Make the correct way the easy way.

notes.intent: Turn the Signals device on the audience and make a concrete, low-friction ask.
notes.summary:
• Read the signals slowly; let each person picture their own workflow.
• Land the reframe, the line to remember: we should spend more time engineering and less time organizing.
• Make the ask concrete: if any of this sounds familiar, message me on Teams or email; let's build it together.
• Then open it up for questions.
notes.bridge: So, what's the workflow you keep dreading? Let's open it up. (hand to Q&A)
